newsitem.title: CHINA: Hainan Airlines seen posting strong listing debut.
newsitem.headline: Hainan Airlines seen posting strong listing debut.

text.p: China's Hainan Airlines Co Ltd will likely post a strong listing debut of its foreign currency B shares on Thursday as investors bank on the backing of U.S. financier George Soros, brokers said on Wednesday.
The airline, which would be China's first domestically listed airline, planned to list 71 million B shares on Thursday with an issue price of 3.90 yuan, or the equivalent of $0.47, per share.
"Investors figure if Soros has a piece of the airline, then there must be something there," said an analyst at a foreign brokerage in Shanghai.
Soros is best know for having made a killing at Britian's expense when he correctly speculated that sterling would be forced out of Europe's exchange rate mechanism in September 1992.
American Aviation Investment, an investment fund partially controlled by Soros, owned 25 percent of the registered share capital of Hainan Airlines, the airline said in a prospectus.

The relatively small float of Hainan Airlines could make the newly listed share the target of speculative buying on Thursday despite current weak market sentiment, an analyst at an Asian securities firm in Shanghai said.
But Hainan Airlines chairman and president Chen Feng said on Wednesday the company was underpinned by solid fundamentals.
"We are different from the others (domestic airlines)," Chen told reporters at a media briefing.
"We have a new management system and our service is better," he said. "For our passengers, it's like being at home."
Hainan Airlines now had a fleet of 13 aircraft, including five Boeing Co 737-300s and four Boeing 737-400s, flying 40 domestic routes, the company's prospectus said.
The airline planned to expand both the size of its fleet and the number of domestic and international routes in order to face fierce industry competition, Chen said.
Hainan Airlines would use the $31.7 million in net proceeds from the issue to buy the facilities and equipment to service three Boeing 767 aircraft which it planned to buy in the future, he said.

The Chinese government had already approved the purchase but no agreement had yet been signed with Boeing BA N, Chen said, adding that Hainan Airlines was considering U.S. export loans or an overseas bond issue to help raise funds to buy the aircraft.
The Chinese carrier also hoped for permission to fly to Hong Kong and Macau in 1998, and to be granted international routes later, he said.
The airline would also seek to expand on its current two tie-ups with hotels around China to diversify into package tours, Chen said.
Hainan Airlines registered profit after tax and minority interests of 89.076 million yuan in 1996 and expected this figure to climb to not less than 140 million for 1997, the prospectus said.
